claims.text: Increasing the cooling rate during processing of a magnetic high-entropy alloy will increase its coercive field.
The conventionally cast baseline alloy has a relatively coarse-grained microstructure.
Rapid cooling immediately after solidification will refine the alloy microstructure and reduce its grain size.
Rapid cooling immediately after solidification will produce a higher density of structural defects.
Grain refinement and quench-induced defects will increase the number of domain-wall pinning sites.
An increased number of domain-wall pinning sites will increase the coercive field.
Rapidly cooled samples will have a statistically significant higher coercive field than matched, slowly cooled samples.
Conventional slower cooling results in a coarser grain structure than rapid cooling.
The predicted effect should hold when alloy composition and processing conditions other than cooling rate are controlled and testing is performed at ambient temperature.
An extremely high cooling rate may produce an amorphous structure.
Formation of an amorphous structure may prevent the proposed coercivity increase.
The alloy composition may limit the extent of grain refinement and thereby limit the intervention's effect.
Structural evolution under rapid quenching in high-entropy alloys may vary with composition.
No direct evidence is provided linking rapid cooling to increased coercivity in magnetic high-entropy alloys.
